title: First Words
subtitle: print, strings, comments, and your first variable

questions.prompt: Which line prints the word hello?
questions.explain: print is a function, so the thing you want shown goes inside its parentheses. echo and printf belong to other languages.

questions.prompt: Build the line that prints hello.
questions.explain: Function name first, then an opening paren, then the value, then the closing paren.

questions.prompt: What appears on screen when this runs?
questions.explain: The quotes mark where the text starts and ends. They are not part of the text itself, so they are not printed.

questions.prompt: Python cares about capital letters. Which one runs?
questions.explain: Python is case sensitive. Print with a capital P is a different name, and Python has no idea what it means.

questions.prompt: Build the line that prints Good morning.
questions.explain: A space inside the quotes is just another character in the text.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of running your first program in order.
questions.explain: Unsaved edits are invisible to Python. Save before you run, every time.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a valid Python string?
questions.explain: A string has to close with the same quote character it opened with. Mixing a double quote and a single quote leaves the string unterminated.

questions.prompt: Build a line that prints:  it's fine
questions.explain: Wrap the text in double quotes and the apostrophe inside causes no trouble. Single quotes would end the string at the apostrophe.

questions.prompt: What does the # symbol do in Python?
options: Starts a comment that Python ignores
Starts a new line of output
answer: Starts a comment that Python ignores
questions.explain: Everything after # on that line is for humans. Python skips it entirely.

questions.prompt: How many lines does this program print?
questions.explain: The first line is a comment, so only the print runs.

questions.prompt: Put a comment above the code it explains.
questions.explain: A comment above the line is the normal Python habit, and it reads like a caption.

questions.prompt: This line has a mistake. What is it?
questions.explain: Python reads to the end of the line looking for the closing quote, does not find one, and raises SyntaxError.

questions.prompt: Which word appears first on screen?
options: They appear at the same time
questions.explain: Python runs a file top to bottom, one line at a time.

questions.prompt: Order the lines so the output reads: ready / steady / go
questions.explain: Output order is line order. Nothing reorders itself.

questions.prompt: What does an empty print() do?
questions.explain: print always ends with a newline, so calling it with nothing inside gives you an empty line, which is how you space output out.

questions.prompt: Build two lines that print hi and then bye.
questions.explain: Two complete calls, each with its own parentheses. The blocks repeat because the code repeats.

questions.prompt: Does Python ever run the last line of a file first?
options: No, it always starts at the top
Yes, if the last line is a print
Yes, files run bottom to top
Only when the file has comments
answer: No, it always starts at the top
questions.explain: A Python file executes top to bottom. Functions can delay when code runs, but the reading order never flips.

questions.prompt: Order these lines to count down 3, 2, 1, liftoff.
questions.explain: Countdown order is just line order. Python has no idea the lines are a countdown, it only runs them from the top down.

questions.prompt: What exactly does this print?
questions.explain: print joins several values with a single space between them by default.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: sep replaces the space that print normally puts between values.

questions.prompt: Build a line that prints:  a-b
questions.explain: sep is a keyword argument, so it goes inside the parentheses after the values, separated by a comma.

questions.prompt: What does end="" change?
options: print stops adding a newline at the end
print stops adding spaces between values
print writes to a file instead of the screen
answer: print stops adding a newline at the end
questions.explain: end is the text print puts after everything else. Set it to an empty string and the next print continues on the same line.

questions.prompt: What appears on screen?
questions.explain: There are no quotes, so Python does the arithmetic first and print receives the number 7.

questions.prompt: Build a line that prints:  2 + 2 = 4
questions.explain: The quoted part is shown literally, the unquoted part is calculated, and print puts a space between them.

questions.prompt: Order the lines so the program prints Pytor.
questions.explain: A name has to exist before you use it. Reversed, this raises NameError.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: Quotes make it literal text. Without quotes, print(name) would show what the variable holds.

questions.prompt: Build a line that greets by name using an f-string.
questions.explain: The f before the quote is what turns {name} into the value. Without it you print the braces literally.

questions.prompt: What happens when this runs?
options: NameError, because age was never given a value
answer: NameError, because age was never given a value
questions.explain: Python has no default value for a name you never assigned. It stops with NameError.

questions.prompt: Order the lines so the program prints 12.
questions.explain: Assigning again replaces the value. The variable holds whatever was put in last before the print.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: The f-string swaps {name} for the value the variable holds at that moment.
